extracted.intended_audience: educators, policymakers, and general readers interested in primary/rural education and cultural policy
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive commentary on what and how peasants and rural labourers should be taught (and what should be avoided) — argues for a narrow, practical curriculum and criticises diffuse, ideological, or purely literary instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit curriculum to practical basics
rubrics_metrics.description: The peasant should be taught only to read, to write, to calculate, with some geography of his country and precepts of hygiene; this is all he needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching a wide range of sciences and abstractions to the peasant is unnecessary and harmful: 'Le bon sens et l'expérience commanderaient d'apprendre seulement au paysan à lire, à écrire, à calculer. Avec quelques notions de la géographie de son pays et quelques préceptes d'hygiène, c'est tout ce qu'il lui faudrait.' The text argues against overburdening rural pupils with notions they will never apply; instruction should be immediately usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid diffuse, heteroclite instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction given 'à tort et à travers' leaves few traces in brains not suited to assimilate it; diffuse programs fail to change peasant mentalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observes that broad, unfocused curricula produce only 'le souvenir d'une contrainte extrême' and that most pupils forget what they were taught once relieved of the pedagogue's authority. Anti-pattern: stuffing the peasant's mind with many unrelated subjects ('un tas de notions') expecting deep absorption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise immediate, tangible application
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach things whose application is immediate and tangible to the peasant rather than abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: planting roasted coffee beans in sand — abstractions won't germinate. Examples to teach: dates of fairs (almanac use), local geography, hygiene rules. The curriculum should favor utility (farming-related skills, measurements, simple arithmetic) over theoretical or aesthetic subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate literacy with moral salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing how to read does not necessarily 'save' a man morally; literacy alone is not a guarantee of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticises dramatic portrayals that make literacy tantamount to moral redemption (e.g., characters who become virtuous simply because they learned to read). It notes counterexamples of virtuous illiterate people and of literate workers whose reading produced chimera or political absurdities. Beware of assuming literacy produces automatic moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about the content of reading
rubrics_metrics.description: What people read matters: poor-quality or inappropriate books can do as much (or more) harm than good; the mere act of reading both bad and good books does not guarantee right judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an artisan who reads Jules Verne and magazines may develop ill-founded ideas; 'les mauvais livres peuvent faire autant de bien que les bons' is questioned. Guidance: ensure reading material is relevant and not misleadingly simplistic or radicalizing; avoid leaving workers to 'go au hasard' among books that foster chimera or intolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using schooling as ideological indoctrination
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should not be employed to instill partisan metaphysical or political systems (e.g., materialist optimism that man is perfectible) because it produces unrealistic citizens detached from practical realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises intellectuals who, convinced of perfectibility, imagine an ideal citizen formed by secular schooling and science. This 'chimera' warps judgment and ignores social reality (alcoholism, crime, poverty). Anti-pattern: curricula that serve as vehicles for ideological conversion rather than practical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and respect vocational/natural dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should respect the peasant's inherited character and place ('Every man in his humour'); do not push everyone to abandon their natural or familial roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues against democratic impulses that tell every person they could profitably abandon their assigned place; instead, training should align with faculties and functions appropriate to one's life and vocation. Overreach leads to rural depopulation and social dislocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect limited aesthetic appreciation from peasants
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume peasants will naturally appreciate poetic sensibilities or fine art; their perceptions are oriented toward practical signs (e.g., weather forecasts) rather than aesthetic nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peasants may find the nightingales' song irritating or fail to 'see' the landscape's beauty; pedagogical attempts to cultivate high aesthetic tastes in peasants are likely to fail and are unnecessary for their role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral instruction belongs to religious authority (author's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secular (laïque) moral instruction is seen as a failure; moral education should be the priest's domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parenthetical claim: 'Il y aurait aussi la morale, et ce devrait être l'affaire du curé. Mais nos dirigeants éclairés ne veulent pas du prêtre.' The author believes laic moral education falls short; implication for curriculum planners: consider local religious structures when thinking about moral formation (note: this is a normative standpoint of the author, historically situated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect general schooling to instill historical or civic memory reliably
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where revolutionary history is taught in schools, rural populations often retain little or none of it; expecting civic consciousness from such instruction is unrealistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the rural postman could not recall the significance of 10 August despite schooling. Practical implication: civic/historical curricula must consider fatigue, daily schedules, and relevance; otherwise the content will be forgotten and have no civic impact.
